pages.text: اختتم في مدينة حلب السورية معرض المهن الحرفية والتراثية القديمة، الذي أُقيم تحت شعار "لكل حرفة تاريخ يُروى"، بمشاركة حرفيين وفنانين وأصحاب مشروعات سعوا إلى إحياء الحرف المهددة بالاندثار، وتطوير منتجاتها بما يجمع بين الأصالة والحداثة، ونقل خبراتها إلى الأجيال الجديدة. وجاء المعرض في إطار مشروع "صون"، الذي ركز على المهن التراثية الحلبية، بهدف الحفاظ على هذا الإرث الثقافي غير المادي، وتعريف الأجيال الجديدة بالحرف القديمة التي ارتبطت بتاريخ المدينة وحياة سكانها، فضلا عن مساعدة العاملين فيها على تطوير مشروعاتهم وتحويل مهاراتهم التقليدية إلى فرص عمل مستدامة. وقالت مديرة المشروع روميسة شيخ، إن العمل بدأ باستقطاب المستفيدين وفق معايير محددة، مع تخصيص النسبة الكبرى من المشاركين للنساء، مقابل 20% للرجال، بهدف مساعدة النساء اللواتي يمارسن الحرف التراثية في المنازل على الانتقال إلى ريادة الأعمال، وتوسيع نطاق أعمالهن لتصل إلى الأسواق. وأوضحت أن المشاركات خضعن لدورات تدريبية تناولت التسويق والتسعير الرقمي، وآليات ترخيص المشروعات، وبناء هوية بصرية مميزة لكل مشروع، بما يساعد صاحبات الحرف على تقديم منتجاتهن بصورة أكثر احترافية والوصول إلى شرائح أوسع من الزبائن. وأضافت شيخ أن المشروع نظم جولات في أسواق حلب القديمة للتعرف إلى تاريخ الحرف وطبيعة ممارستها، قبل إقامة المعرض الختامي على مدى 3 ليال، في موقع اُختير بمحيط قلعة حلب ، بما يتناسب مع الهوية التاريخية للمكان وطبيعة المبادرة التي تمحورت حول التراث وسبل الحفاظ عليه. وتراوحت أعمار المشاركين بين 17 و60 عاما، في دلالة على اهتمام فئات عمرية مختلفة بالحرف التقليدية، ورغبة أجيال جديدة في تعلمها وتطويرها. ومن بين المشاركين في المعرض الفنان التشكيلي والنحات على الخشب أحمد هنداوي الذي عمل على إحياء هذه الحرفة التي باتت مهددة بالاندثار، من خلال إدخالها إلى مجالي الديكور والخط العربي، وتقديم أعمال جمعت بين التقنيات التقليدية واللمسات الفنية الحديثة. وأوضح هنداوي أنه سعى إلى نقل النحت على الخشب من الاستخدامات التقليدية المرتبطة بالأثاث إلى إنتاج قطع فنية يمكن اقتناؤها بوصفها لوحات تزين المنازل، بما يمنح الحرفة أبعادا جمالية جديدة ويسهم في الحفاظ على جانب من تراث حلب الصناعي والفني. وأشار إلى أن المدينة كانت رائدة في مجال النحت على الخشب خلال الفترة الممتدة من سبعينيات القرن الماضي إلى تسعينياته، معربا عن أمله في استعادة هذه المكانة، ليس من خلال إقامة المعارض فحسب، بل عبر إنشاء أماكن متخصصة لتعليم الحرفة وتحويلها إلى مادة دراسية أو منهج تدريبي يتيح للشباب تعلمها وتطويرها وإضافة أفكار جديدة إليها. بدورها، عرضت الحرفية المتخصصة في المكرمية رغد وزان تجربتها في تطوير هذه الحرفة التراثية وتوسيع استخداماتها. وأوضحت أن المكرمية ارتبطت تاريخيا بصناعة شبكات الصيد لدى البحارة، الذين كانوا يستغلون رحلاتهم الطويلة في إنجاز قطع يدوية، فيما اشتهرت في حلب باستخدامها في صناعة حاملات النباتات. وقالت رغد إنها عملت على تطوير منتجات المكرمية لتشمل الديكورات والمستلزمات المنزلية المتنوعة، وإعادة إدخالها إلى البيوت الحلبية، لما تمنحه من إحساس بالدفء والنعومة، فضلا عن تعريف الشباب والأطفال بتاريخ الحرفة وتشجيعهم على ابتكار تصاميم جديدة مستوحاة منها. وأبدت إحدى زائرات المعرض اعتزازها باستمرار الحرف اليدوية في المدينة، بعدما اعتقد كثيرون أنها مهددة بالاختفاء، مشيدة بالدعم الذي يحظى به الحرفيون وبالدقة الفنية التي ظهرت في المنتجات المعروضة. وقالت إن النحت على الخشب كان من أبرز الأعمال التي لفتت انتباهها، لما يتسم به من دقة وتفاصيل فنية تعكس روح الحرفي الذي أنجز القطعة، معربة عن أملها أن تصل المنتجات التراثية الحلبية إلى الأسواق الخارجية، بما يعزز حضور المدينة بوصفها مركزا عريقا للحرف والأصالة. وشكل المعرض مساحة لعرض المهارات التقليدية أمام الجمهور، وفرصة لربط الحرفيين بالأسواق الحديثة، في محاولة للحفاظ على الموروث الحرفي الحلبي وضمان استمراره عبر الأجيال، مع تطويره بما يتناسب مع متطلبات الحياة المعاصرة.

cards.headline: Cries of forgotten farmers: No compensation on Accra-Kumasi Expressway - Graphic Online

image.alt: Cries of forgotten farmers: No compensation on Accra-Kumasi Expressway - Graphic Online

pages.text: I write anonymously on behalf of hundreds of desperate farmers whose livelihoods have been impaired due to the construction of the Accra-Kumasi Expressway. Months ago, officials cleared our farms, destroying our cocoa, food crops and oil palms. We stepped aside willingly because we were promised prompt, fair compensation. While the media recently reported that a first tranche of payments was made to over 450 farmers, a massive, forgotten number of us have received absolutely nothing. Our lands are gone, we have no alternative incomes, and our children's school fees are due. When we try to ask for updates, we are met with total silence. The Ministry of Roads and Highways, the Ghana Highway Authority and the Land Valuation Division have become completely unreachable. Development should not destroy the citizens it claims to serve. You cannot take a farmer’s only source of survival and abandon them. We appeal to the media to investigate this delay. We urge the Minister of Roads and Highways and the project coordinators to break their silence and immediately publish a clear, transparent payment schedule for those of us left behind.

cards.headline: NATO commander says the alliance does not want war but is 'ready to fight tonight'

image.alt: NATO commander says the alliance does not want war but is 'ready to fight tonight'

pages.text:
Gen. Alexus Grynkewich aims to send a clear signal to the Kremlin that the alliance will resist any attack. NATO’s top commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade . “Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.” The rare intervention by the four-star general to discuss a military blueprint underscores NATO’s effort to deter Russia. It is also aimed at sending a message of NATO unity after a grueling year for the alliance, which was rocked by Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland and infighting over the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran . Under the three-part blueprint, NATO would initially use land-based troops — buttressed by air, naval, cyber and space capabilities — to stop an assault, targeting attacking forces and preventing them from seizing territory, Grynkewich said. NATO would then use sensors and autonomous systems among other capabilities to “overwhelm enemy formations … and their advance,” he said, before using “highly effective precision munitions” and unmanned systems if necessary to “break the [enemy] warfighting system” and “everything that supports” it. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the theory laid out by Grynkewich “will send a strong message to our adversaries that we are going to defend ourselves.” NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe said he does “not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable.” But “we will … ensure any attack against any ally proves utterly futile.” The speech describes a more forceful response if a foe attacks, but its credibility depends on allies having the forces, infrastructure, and coordination to implement the plan. Asked whether the plan factored in a scenario where the U.S. was engaged elsewhere, Grynkewich said: “It absolutely does account for that, and in fact, it must.” Under Trump, the U.S. has sought to refocus its military on other priorities such as the Indo-Pacific, homeland security and the Western Hemisphere. U.S. ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said in Warsaw on Monday that Europe only ranks fourth among Washington’s strategic concerns. The Pentagon has already cut its contributions to NATO crisis forces and is set to unveil a review of U.S. forces in Europe by the end of the year. “No one should question the commitment of the United States to this alliance,” Grynkewich argued, but added that “ultimately, it's a political decision about who's providing troops where.” Camille Grand, NATO's former assistant secretary-general for defense investment, said the plan was “a very deliberate effort” to signal that the alliance would be ready to fight with or without large-scale involvement of U.S. forces. “For my country, fighting with Russians is with or without Americans,” said a separate senior European defense official, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “We expect them to come, but if they won’t, we will fight anyway.” Grand added that the blueprint is also an indication that NATO is ready to take a bolder approach toward Moscow by threatening the destruction of its war machine even deep behind the front lines. That comes as Moscow sent a letter to NATO last month threatening to use its nuclear arsenal if the alliance tried to isolate its Kaliningrad exclave. Grynkewich warned that NATO would be ready to respond — even with its nuclear arsenal. “Should an adversary threaten escalation by saber-rattling, or should one actually decide to escalate during conflict, it will not fracture our alliance,” he said. “We should take comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects and the implicit warning that we could match any enemy move up the escalation ladder.” Italy is hosting NATO’s annual nuclear exercise, which starts next week. European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport. If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S. General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw Monday. Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called NATO's "Theory of Victory." The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings." Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack NATO is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces. But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said NATO's combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground. "My theory of victory is simple," he told the Warsaw conference. "We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us." That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said. In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the NATO alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent. Denmark's defense intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the NATO alliance. But, at the same time, President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try lower prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections. "Ultimately it's a political decision," as to where troops are deployed but "no one should question the U.S. commitment to the alliance," Grynkewich said. It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a "coherent" response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow "where our red lines are." The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine. While Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning to escalate with drone or rocket strikes on European allies supporting Ukraine, other countries have called for calm. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Agency said there is a "low but growing risk" that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia. NATO does not seek war with anyone but will see a military attack coming and "is unlikely to be caught by surprise," Grynkewich said. Although Grynkewich said NATO would defend against any attack by Russia using a network of sensors and autonomous systems, some NATO nations have previously struggled to perform in exercises simulating drone warfare. They have also faced challenges detecting and responding to incursions of drones which have entered their airspace. Multiple attack drones have crashed in NATO countries bordering Russia, Ukraine and Belarus. And in May, residents in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius were told to seek shelter after a drone strayed into Lithuanian airspace. When asked if NATO could deter Russia in the way Grynkewich described, his spokesperson, Col. The network that connects systems to shoot down drones and sensors is in the process of being established, although they have not yet taken down any drones, he said. acceptedSources.evidenceText: Emma Burrows, Associated Press Emma Burrows, Associated Press WARSAW, Poland (AP) — NATO's top military commander said the alliance is "ready to fight tonight" if it is attacked, as European officials warn Russia could test NATO's defenses with increased covert attacks or a limited military incursion. European nations have in recent months faced an escalation of covert Russian activity, including an arson attack on an Estonian defense company and a failed attempt to attack a Ukrainian aircraft at a German airport. If Russia decides to attack NATO, the alliance will respond by using sensors, autonomous systems and military force to stop any assault, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander U.S. General Alexus Grynkewich said in Warsaw Monday. Grynkewich spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum to set out what he called NATO's "Theory of Victory." The NATO commander said he does not believe that a conflict is imminent or inevitable and that the most effective way to preserve peace is to prepare for war and to maintain open lines of communication to "resolve misunderstandings." Grynkewich provided no specific details about what kind of attack NATO is preparing for, nor where, nor with what kind of forces. But outlining what a response to a Russian attack could look like, Grynkewich said NATO's combined land, sea and air forces will move to stop Moscow seizing territory and deny Russia the ability to hold ground. "My theory of victory is simple," he told the Warsaw conference. "We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. And if required, we will break the enemy's forces and the operational war-fighting system arrayed against us." That includes not just the attacking force but anything and everything that supports, sustains and controls it, he said. In recent weeks, senior European officials and intelligence services have warned that Russia may be planning to test the NATO alliance with increased covert attacks or even an incursion after a spate of sabotage incidents across the continent. Denmark's defense intelligence service specifically warned Russia could use such tactics to split the NATO alliance. But, at the same time, President Donald Trump has also sent shock waves through Europe by agreeing to a deal to buy diesel from Russia in a bid to try lower prices in the U.S. ahead of the midterm elections. WATCH: Poland braces for potential confrontation as Russia tests NATO defenses Earlier this year, the U.S. president said he was pulling American troops from Europe and his war with Iran has led to critical shortages of advanced air defense missiles in Europe. "Ultimately it's a political decision," as to where troops are deployed but "no one should question the U.S. commitment to the alliance," Grynkewich said. It is important, Grynkewich said, that alliance members coordinate a "coherent" response to Russian activity to make it clear to Moscow "where our red lines are." The response to increased Russian malign activity and sabotage, he said, should be to double down on support for Ukraine. While Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia is planning to escalate with drone or rocket strikes on European allies supporting Ukraine, other countries have called for calm. Denmark's Defense Intelligence Agency said there is a "low but growing risk" that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia. NATO does not seek war with anyone but will see a military attack coming and "is unlikely to be caught by surprise," Grynkewich said. They have also faced challenges detecting and responding to incursions of drones which have entered their airspace. In its assessment released earlier in September, Denmark's defense intelligence service suggested Russia could try to acquire Ukrainian drones and use them to attack Europe, in order to obfuscate any Russian involvement. Tusk suggested Russia will likely pretend any attacks are "accidental" in order to "paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries" to rush to the defense of a member state coming under attack. The Danish service said the aim of any such attack would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine and sow division in NATO. But both the Danish service and O'Donnell said while Russia is fighting in Ukraine, it would be difficult to launch an outright attack on NATO. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed,” he said. “We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any Ally, proves utterly futile.”Endorsed by all 32 NATO members, the plan combines conventional military capabilities, including ground forces, and military hardware, with advanced technologies such as drones, counter-drone systems and artificial intelligence.It also draws on lessons from modern warfare, particularly the fighting on the ground and in the skies over Ukraine. “We're learning a tonne from Ukrainian partners,” Grynkewich told the forum.Three stages of defence: block, blunt and breakThe strategy rests on three principles — “block”, “blunt” and “break” — which Grynkewich described as simple but central to NATO’s approach.“We will block the initial attack. If the attack persists, we will blunt it and prevent any enemy advance. forces from seizing allied territory.NATO ground troops would engage advancing formations, contain their movements and destroy forces attempting to push into alliance territory.“We will fix the enemy formations and deny the seizure of Alliance territory,” Grynkewich said. “Land-based forces will attack the enemy and destroy his advancing forces,” he added.Blunt: stop further attacksIf an initial threats with limited or no direct human intervention.Grynkewich said the strategy would combine capabilities across multiple operational domains to prevent enemy forces from making further advances.Break: disable the enemy’s ability to fightThe final phase would target not only enemy troops but also the systems that allow them to operate.These would include command structures, supply The attack occurred at approximately 11:15 a.m. Russian forces used a Smerch multiple-launch rocket system equipped with a cluster warhead, according to Donetsk Oblast Governor Vadym Filashkin. Four other people were injured, including an 18-year-old man and three older men, police said. Nearby homes were also damaged. “One strike destroyed the lives of an entire family,” Filashkin wrote on Telegram. The governor accused Russian forces of deliberately targeting residential areas with cluster munitions to inflict maximum civilian casualties. He renewed his appeal to families with children to evacuate from dangerous areas of Donetsk Oblast rather than wait for another attack. Speaking to a gathering of European security officials in Warsaw on Monday, the Ukrainian president said Kyiv would retaliate if strikes on its power grid continued: “If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire this winter, we will respond.” On Sunday, Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Kyiv and Moscow that Zelenskyy said neither side had agreed to. On Monday, Zelenskyy said he was “surprised” by the post, which went online while Kyiv was being attacked by Russian Shahed drones. Russia then launched a “targeted attack” on a Kharkiv power station hours later, as much of Kyiv was plunged into darkness. “It’s clear that Putin does not read Truth Social,” Zelenskyy said. Russia bombed six energy facilities on Monday, injuring 33 people, the Ukrainian president said. “It is becoming increasingly clear that Russia does not want to agree to the energy ceasefire proposed by the US and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our communities,” he added. Zelenskyy also suggested that Ukraine’s recent counter-strikes on datacentres belonging to the Russian technology company Yandex had reduced the number of bots posting messages in Europe and the US. “It suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social platforms. There was less hate, less division and fewer provocations,” he said. The Kremlin refused to say on Monday whether it agreed with Trump’s Truth Social post, which claimed a ceasefire was “effective immediately”. It also rejected Zelenskyy’s proposal that Russia stop bombing for 60 days so Ukraine could hold a presidential election. Moscow wanted an overall peace deal first, it said, which, for the Kremlin, means Kyiv’s capitulation. The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday, when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports . He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections. Both Republican and Democratic politicians have criticised the move, pointing out that the deal violates a US law that blocks Russian energy imports. On Monday Trump defended it. “I made the right choice for the American People – ALWAYS, AMERICA FIRST!” he wrote in a social media post. Earlier a furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader” , he said on Saturday. Ukraine has said it is ready to negotiate an energy ceasefire that would take the pressure off its electricity grid before the winter. European leaders have voiced support for Kyiv in its dispute with Washington, saying Russia was responsible for the continuing strikes on energy infrastructure in both countries. “We welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds,” the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said at a meeting of European foreign ministers on Monday. “We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.” Ministers from the Baltic states criticised a US decision to lift sanctions on imports of Russian diesel , which had been blocked as part of punishment for Putin launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. “This deal doesn’t help, neither the crisis of the oil products, nor the unity within the transatlantic community when it concerns Russia,” said Lithuania’s foreign minister, Keʂtutis Budrys. “And it is not the European way. Our way is to increase pressure because we already see how it works.” Russia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles ahead of the cold winter months, leading to blackouts and water shortages far earlier in the season than has been usual during the war. Trump’s proposal was for both sides to halt strikes on oil refineries but Kallas said that deal favoured Russia, which has far more refineries. The US president has blamed the high price of diesel on Ukraine’s attacks, rather than the global shock to energy markets from the US war in Iran and the subsequent closure of the strait of Hormuz. According to the Financial Times, the US ⁠has threatened ⁠to stop ​the procurement ⁠system that provides ⁠Ukraine ​with ‌weapons, paid for by its European allies. The White House has also said it could turn off intelligence sharing unless Kyiv halts its ‌long-range strikes on ​Russian oil refineries. The Kyiv Independent newspaper said Ukraine’s commander in chief, Mykhailo Drapatyi, had received a call from the US telling him to stop bombing. “They called all the top military officials with threats,” a Ukrainian official told the newspaper. Ben Hodges, the former head of US forces in Europe, described the energy ceasefire “deal” as a fantasy and “a classic ‘Trumpian’ announcement of something not based on any facts.” “No one should be misled,” he said, adding that Russia “never adheres to any agreements unless forced to do so”. He urged Ukraine’s military to ignore Trump and “ramp up” their attacks on Russian oil and gas complexes. “Clearly, this is having a very significant effect. Otherwise, you wouldn’t be hearing all this pressure from the Kremlin on the White House demanding that it stop. Of course, it is having a huge impact.”

image.alt: A headscarf at the school gates: the dispute over hijab and the future of Azerbaijani girls

pages.text:
In October 1901, the Alexandrinsky Russian-Muslim School for Girls — the first Muslim girls’ school in the Caucasus — opened in Baku with funding from oil industrialist and philanthropist Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev. Dressed in black, Taghiyev stands in the centre among the pupils and teachers of the Baku Muslim Girls’ School. New school uniform requirements have once again brought Azerbaijan’s secular tradition into conflict with the religious beliefs of some families. But behind the dispute over clothing lies a simpler question: how can every girl be kept in education? In videos shared on social media, schoolgirls wearing headscarves leave school in tears: they have been denied entry to lessons. The voices of the pupils themselves are heard far less often in the public debate than declarations about their future. A headscarf alone cannot reveal whether a girl wears it out of personal conviction, family custom or pressure. Nor can her tears establish every cause of the conflict. That is why any solution must begin with a conversation with the child, rather than assigning someone else’s position to her. For some parents, what is happening has already become a question of access to education. One parent in Sumgayit told AzadlıqRadiosu : “Our children are not being allowed into school because of our religious beliefs.” This is a parent’s testimony, rather than a fact established by a court. But it identifies these families’ central fear: a clothing requirement could mean missed lessons. The current dispute gained fresh momentum following Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 309 of September 21, 2026. It added a prohibition to the school uniform rules on clothing elements that undermine the uniform’s consistency and do not comply with the principle of secular general education. Yet the word “hijab” does not appear in the document. Questions of compliance have been assigned to schools’ pedagogical councils , while parents are required to ensure that their children follow the rules. National dress, or elements of it, may be worn at events dedicated to Azerbaijan’s history and culture with the permission of the pedagogical council. The distinction between the resolution’s wording and its practical application matters. The document establishes clothing requirements, but contains no explicit provision barring pupils from lessons specifically for wearing hijab. Each such case therefore requires separate examination: who made the decision, on what grounds, in what form, and how can the family appeal?
